analysis.one_liner: Applies Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes to income above $400,000.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote in the House Ways and Means Committee before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, the Social Security payroll tax stops applying to wages once they pass a yearly cap, so a worker earning $160,000 pays it on every dollar while a worker earning $2 million pays it on the same capped amount, and business profits paid out to owners avoid payroll tax entirely. This bill applies Social Security payroll taxes to wages between the cap and $400,000, adds a 1.2% Medicare tax on wage and self-employment income above $400,000 ($500,000 for couples), and taxes the pass-through business income and investment income of people making over $400,000. All of the new money goes directly into the Social Security and Medicare trust funds.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future Social Security and Medicare beneficiaries, since the new revenue shores up trust funds that are otherwise projected to face shortfalls; also workers generally, because closing the gap in payroll taxation spreads the program's funding across high earners rather than capping it. People earning under $400,000 owe none of the new taxes, except wages between the current cap and $400,000, which is above the earnings of most workers.
analysis.who_pays: People and households with income above $400,000: high earners pay Social Security tax on wages between the current cap and $400,000 plus a 1.2% Medicare tax above $400,000, and owners of pass-through businesses (law firms, hedge funds, real estate partnerships) pay tax on their share of business profits above the threshold.
analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is durable program funding spread onto people with the most income; the cost falls almost entirely on households above $400,000, though some of them are professionals and small business owners rather than the very wealthy, and the higher tax on trusts and estates is steep. A fair objection is that taxing the gap between the current cap and $400,000 raises taxes on some upper-middle earners, not only the rich.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Ways and Means Committee, got shuffled to two subcommittees at the end of 2024, and never received a markup or floor vote before the Congress ended.
outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners and pass-through business owners above the $400,000 threshold, who will not pay the new taxes; the trust-fund shortfall remains unaddressed.

for.name: Rep. Brendan F. Boyle (D-PA)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Ways and Means Committee.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over payroll and investment income taxes
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Health and the Subcommittee on Social Security in December 2024 and never scheduled a markup or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and both cosponsors were House Democrats, and the bill received no Republican cosponsors.
